messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had been a social media manager for a relief agency, a job that once felt a world away from the front lines. That changed nine months ago in a dusty, sun-baked compound where he was coordinating aid distribution. The attack was brutally fast. The screech of tires, the shouting, the sudden, concussive blast that threw him against a container wall. He remembers the chaos, the smells of dust and cordite, and a paralyzing moment of indecision when he was supposed to be directing people to safety. He froze. That moment, a brief synaptic failure under impossible pressure, had become the anchor point of his new reality.

In the months after his return to the U.S., what gnawed at him most was the silence that followed. The men who overran the compound had faced no consequences; they had simply vanished back into the conflict. This profound sense of injustice, the belief that what happened was deeply unfair and that the world was a place where such acts went unpunished, began to curdle into a constant, pervasive sense of threat. If that could happen with no accountability, Kofi reasoned, then safety was an illusion and danger could erupt from anywhere, at any time. This conviction left his nervous system on a permanent, humming alert. Back in his quiet suburban home, he found himself unable to concentrate on a book or a conversation with his wife, his attention always snagged by a floorboard creaking upstairs or the sound of an unfamiliar car idling on the street. He became superalert, a man perpetually on guard in a world he no longer trusted.

The exhaustion of being so constantly watchful was immense. To manage the feeling of being a live wire, always ready to jump at a slamming door or a sudden notification tone from the work phone he now dreaded, Kofi developed a set of rigid, silent rules. This was his attempt to regain control, to manage a world that felt menacingly unpredictable. At his open-plan office, he would only work at a desk in the corner, where he could see all the entrances. He would constantly scan his surroundings, tracking the movements of colleagues, a habit he knew was irrational but couldn't stop. Most of all, he tried to avoid thinking about the event, pushing the memories away whenever they surfaced. He would detach himself from them, speaking of the attack in a flat, third-person monotone as if it had happened to someone else, a desperate strategy to keep the terror at bay.

But these strategies only seemed to tighten the coil of his anxiety. The constant checking of his surroundings only served to confirm his belief in imminent danger; every person walking too quickly, every unexpected noise became proof that he was right to be on guard, which in turn amplified his hypervigilance. The very act of scanning for threats made the world feel more threatening. Similarly, his attempts to suppress the memories made them more intrusive. They would ambush him without warning—the smell of diesel fuel from a passing truck, a shout from a nearby construction site—and the sensory fragments would slam into him, raw and terrifying. This proved to him that the danger wasn't just outside, but inside him too, a part of himself he couldn't rely on or control.

His life has shrunk. The job he once loved now feels like a minefield of digital triggers. He can no longer manage the agency's field accounts, the images from the region too potent a reminder. His concentration is so poor that he rereads the same email five times, his mind always drifting back to threat assessment. The final straw came last week when his wife, trying to wake him gently from a nightmare, touched his shoulder and he flinched away with a shout, his heart hammering against his ribs. Seeing the fear in her eyes made him realize he was losing not just himself, but the person he loved most. Kofi has come to therapy because he is terrified that the man he was before the attack is gone for good, and he is desperate to find a way to trust himself, and the world, enough to finally stand down.
